passage.title: Blue Ribbon Peaches
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
I held the warm ceramic baking dish with both oven mitts as Mom opened the screen door of the county fair pavilion. Inside the bright hall, long tables gleamed with white paper cloths and rows of fancy desserts. Right away, my stomach did a nervous flip. The other bakers had brought towering three-layer cakes topped with spun sugar curls and glossy fruit tarts that looked like museum art. My entry was Aunt Delia's skillet peach cobbler, baked in a scratched blue dish that had seen twenty summers.

As I walked to Table Four, I wished I had piped whipped cream roses around the edge to hide the rustic crust. Unlike those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting, my cobbler had a bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks. I set my dish beside a tall chocolate pie and quickly stepped back behind the rope. Soon the three judges walked over with their clipboards. I stared down at my shoes and waited for them to pass right by my plain square pan.

First, the head judge in the red apron tasted the tall cakes at the end of the row. She took polite little bites and wrote short notes on her pad without smiling. Then the judges stopped in front of my scratched blue dish. The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon. As soon as she tasted the warm fruit and crisp crust, her eyebrows rose in surprise.

Instead of moving on, she tapped her spoon against the dish and asked the other two judges to try a bite right away. I watched in shock as all three judges smiled and nodded together. The head judge looked across the rope, spotted the flour smudge on my sleeve, and gave me a warm wink. She said that fancy frosting looks pretty under bright lights, but nothing beats fresh Georgia peaches baked until the crust sings.

Ten minutes later, a shiny blue ribbon for First Place Youth Baking hung beside Aunt Delia's old dish. Walking out into the sunny fairgrounds, I felt silly for doubting our family recipe just because it lacked tall sugar curls. My plain cobbler did not need to copy a store window to be special. Sharing the honest flavor of home had been my strongest asset all along.

tier2Words.definition: a large open building or hall used for fairs, shows, and community events
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin papilio, meaning 'large tent or butterfly wing'
tier2Words.contextClue: Mom opened the screen door of the county fair hall where long tables held rows of desserts.

tier2Words.definition: simple, homemade, and natural in style rather than fancy or polished
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin rus, meaning 'countryside or farm'
tier2Words.contextClue: Unlike the smooth bakery cakes, the cobbler had a simple, bumpy golden top in an old family dish.

tier2Words.definition: tasted or tried a small portion of food to judge its quality
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French essample, meaning 'small test piece'
tier2Words.contextClue: The head judge used a silver spoon to taste a bite of the warm fruit and crisp crust.

tier2Words.definition: a valuable strength or useful quality that helps someone succeed
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French asez, meaning 'enough or valuable resource'
tier2Words.contextClue: Sharing the honest flavor of home turned out to be the narrator's greatest strength in the contest.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who or what sampled the golden peach cobbler?

options.text: The head judge sampled the golden peach cobbler with a silver spoon.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by the head judge' right after 'was eagerly sampled' shows that the head judge is the person who tasted the golden peach cobbler with a silver spoon.

options.text: The golden peach cobbler sampled the silver spoon on Table Four.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action in a silly way! A peach cobbler is a dessert in a baking dish—it cannot taste a silver spoon.

options.text: A pinch of grated nutmeg sampled the fresh lemon peel.
options.childFeedback: Nutmeg and fresh lemon peel are just the spices used to season the cobbler; the head judge is the one who sampled the dish.

options.text: Aunt Delia sampled the three-layer cake behind the rope.
options.childFeedback: Aunt Delia is only mentioned because the narrator used her family recipe and old blue dish; the head judge is the one tasting the entries.

questions.provingSentenceText: The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by the head judge' right after 'was eagerly sampled' shows that the head judge is the person who tasted the golden peach cobbler with a silver spoon.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The golden peach cobbler' receives the action, while 'by the head judge' identifies the actor who sampled it.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words 'was eagerly sampled by the head judge' in Paragraph 3 to see who did the tasting.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 2:

"As I walked to Table Four, I wished I had piped whipped cream roses around the edge to hide the rustic crust. Unlike those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting, my cobbler had a bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks."

What does the word rustic mean as it is used in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Burned black and impossible to eat
options.childFeedback: The cobbler is not burned black—Paragraph 2 describes its 'bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks.'

options.text: Simple and homemade rather than fancy
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'rustic' means simple and homemade rather than fancy, because the narrator contrasts her bumpy golden cobbler crust with the smooth frosting on tall bakery cakes.

options.text: Covered in tall spun sugar curls
options.childFeedback: The other bakers' three-layer cakes had spun sugar curls in Paragraph 1, whereas the narrator's rustic cobbler had a plain, bumpy golden crust.

options.text: Frozen solid inside an ice chest
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says the narrator held the warm ceramic baking dish with oven mitts, so the cobbler was warm, not frozen solid.

questions.provingSentenceText: Unlike those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting, my cobbler had a bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'rustic' means simple and homemade rather than fancy, because the narrator contrasts her bumpy golden cobbler crust with the smooth frosting on tall bakery cakes.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts the 'rustic crust' with 'those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting,' showing that 'rustic' means simple, natural, and homemade.
questions.retryHint: Look at the contrast in Paragraph 2 between 'those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting' and the narrator's bumpy golden crust.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 1, why does the narrator feel nervous as soon as she walks into the county fair pavilion?

options.text: She realizes she forgot to add nutmeg and lemon peel to her peach cobbler.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 confirms that her cobbler was seasoned with grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, so she did not forget those ingredients.

options.text: She drops the warm ceramic dish on the floor before reaching Table Four.
options.childFeedback: She carries the warm dish safely with both oven mitts and sets it on Table Four in Paragraph 2 without dropping it.

options.text: She sees fancy cakes and tarts that make her family's cobbler look plain by comparison.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that the narrator's stomach does a nervous flip when she sees the other bakers' towering three-layer cakes and glossy tarts that make her cobbler in a scratched dish look plain.

options.text: She learns that youth bakers are only allowed to enter chocolate pies in the contest.
options.childFeedback: The table has three-layer cakes, fruit tarts, a chocolate pie, and her peach cobbler—there is no rule allowing only chocolate pies.

questions.provingSentenceText: The other bakers had brought towering three-layer cakes topped with spun sugar curls and glossy fruit tarts that looked like museum art.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 explains that the narrator's stomach does a nervous flip when she sees the other bakers' towering three-layer cakes and glossy tarts that make her cobbler in a scratched dish look plain.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 1, the narrator's stomach does a nervous flip because the other entries are fancy three-layer cakes and glossy tarts that look like museum art compared to her cobbler in a scratched dish.
questions.retryHint: Read the sentences right after 'my stomach did a nervous flip' in Paragraph 1 to see what the other bakers brought.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator's first-person point of view influence how the events at the baking contest are described?

options.text: It proves that the narrator does not care at all about winning a ribbon at the county fair.
options.childFeedback: Her nervous stomach flip in Paragraph 1 and her wish for whipped cream roses in Paragraph 2 show she cares deeply about how her cobbler will be judged.

options.text: It reveals the exact scores that each of the three judges writes down on their private clipboards.
options.childFeedback: Because the story is told from the narrator's point of view behind the rope, she only sees the judges write short notes—not their private clipboard scores.

options.text: It explains the step-by-step history of how the county fair pavilion was built twenty summers ago.
options.childFeedback: The twenty summers in Paragraph 1 describe how old Aunt Delia's scratched blue baking dish is, not the building history of the fair pavilion.

options.text: It lets the reader experience the narrator's secret doubts about her plain dish before she discovers how much the judges love its taste.
options.childFeedback: Because the narrator tells the story in the first person ('I wished,' 'my stomach did a nervous flip'), we get to feel her private doubts about her plain dish before the judges surprise her with praise.

questions.provingSentenceText: As I walked to Table Four, I wished I had piped whipped cream roses around the edge to hide the rustic crust.
questions.childTip: Because the narrator tells the story in the first person ('I wished,' 'my stomach did a nervous flip'), we get to feel her private doubts about her plain dish before the judges surprise her with praise.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the story is told from the baker's first-person ('I') perspective (ELAGSE5RL6), readers directly share her initial insecurity about her cobbler's appearance and her surprise when its flavor wins first place.
questions.retryHint: Think about what the narrator shares in Paragraphs 1 and 2 ('my stomach did a nervous flip,' 'I wished...') that only she would know.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central theme of the story?

options.text: True quality and honest family traditions matter more than flashy outward appearances.
options.childFeedback: The story teaches that honest homemade quality matters more than flashy looks: even without spun sugar curls or a new pan, the fresh peach cobbler wins first place for its delicious flavor.

options.text: Three-layer cakes with spun sugar curls never taste good at a summer fair.
options.childFeedback: The head judge says fancy frosting looks pretty under bright lights, not that three-layer cakes never taste good.

options.text: Bakers must always buy brand-new ceramic dishes if they want to impress county fair judges.
options.childFeedback: The narrator wins First Place Youth Baking using Aunt Delia's scratched twenty-year-old dish, proving a baker does not need a brand-new pan to win.

options.text: Whipped cream roses are the easiest way to fix a dessert that has a bumpy crust.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, the narrator feels silly for ever wishing she had hidden her crust, realizing her plain cobbler did not need fancy decorations.

questions.provingSentenceText: She said that fancy frosting looks pretty under bright lights, but nothing beats fresh Georgia peaches baked until the crust sings.
questions.childTip: The story teaches that honest homemade quality matters more than flashy looks: even without spun sugar curls or a new pan, the fresh peach cobbler wins first place for its delicious flavor.
questions.parentExplanation: Both the head judge's remark in Paragraph 4 and the narrator's reflection in Paragraph 5 highlight the theme that genuine quality ('honest flavor of home') outshines flashy surface decoration.
questions.retryHint: Look at what the head judge says in Paragraph 4 and what the narrator realizes in Paragraph 5 about fancy looks versus honest flavor.
